lesson_title: The Peg, the Twins and the Echo
hook_text: Tie two ropes from one peg to a round wall. They're ALWAYS the same length. Here's the theorem hiding in that.
clip_script: Drive a peg into the ground outside a circular kraal, and run two ropes from it to just touch the wall on either side. Measure them. Identical. Move the peg anywhere — closer, further, off to the side — and the two ropes stay perfect twins, every single time. That's a theorem: tangents from the same point are equal, and the reason is a mirror. The line from your peg to the centre is a line of symmetry, so each rope is the other one's reflection. Now watch the theorem pay out. Equal ropes mean the peg and the two touch-points form an isosceles triangle — and isosceles triangles hand you equal base angles for free. Fifty-two degrees at the peg? The leftover one twenty-eight splits into sixty-four and sixty-four at the wall. Then comes the strangest theorem in the chapter: each of those sixty-fours is an angle between a tangent and a chord, and it echoes — straight across the chord to the far side of the circle, where every spectator on that arc sees exactly sixty-four degrees. Twins, isosceles, echo: three sentences, and you've just solved a full-length rider. The hardest circle questions in the book are built from exactly these three moves.
visual_style: A top-down kraal circle with a peg and two ropes snapping taut to equal lengths; a mirror line flashing down the middle; angle values popping in — 52, then 64 and 64 — and a glowing arc catching the echoed 64 on the far side.
mood: Playful and revelatory — farmyard picture turning into serious geometry.
pacing: Quick hook on the equal ropes, steady beat through the isosceles payout, dramatic pause before the echo lands.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and solve riders with three sentences.
